body.heading: A profession of pencils
paragraphs: From the 1700s into the mid-1900s, a computer was a person. Governments, astronomers and engineers employed rooms of them to produce the tables everyone depended on: tide tables, navigation charts, artillery ranges, planetary positions. The work was split into small steps, checked by doing it twice, and carried out with pencils, paper and mechanical adding machines.
Many of these computers were women, hired because they were skilled and — in the unfair economics of the time — cheaper. Their names rarely appeared on the publications their numbers made possible.

body.heading: The Harvard and NASA computers
paragraphs: At Harvard Observatory, women computers measured and classified hundreds of thousands of stars from photographic plates; their work produced the classification system for stars still used today. At NASA and its predecessor, teams of women mathematicians calculated flight paths for rockets and astronauts.

Katherine Johnson, one of the most celebrated, personally checked the electronic computer's numbers for John Glenn's first American orbital flight in 1962 — at his request. 'If she says they're good,' Glenn said, 'then I'm ready to go.'

body.heading: The handover to machines
paragraphs: Electronic computers took the job title along with the job. The human teams faded, though their methods — dividing work, double-checking, writing steps others could repeat — became the foundations of programming itself.
Remembering them restores something important: computing was never only about machines. It began as people being careful together, at scale, with pencils.

takeaway: Before machines, 'computers' were people — often uncredited women — whose careful arithmetic carried astronomy and the first spaceflights.
